However, it is stated in general that what is conceived as a hare is not the moon,
because it possesses substantial existence,
just like the sun, stars, and so forth.
Although the reason and the example are correct,
the thesis contradicts worldly convention;
therefore, it is called a fallacy.
However, the treatise provides only the thesis (*pakṣa*) and the reason (*hetu*), but lacks the example (*dṛṣṭānta*). The *Nyāyamukha* states:
"Furthermore, if within this [reasoning] it is due to being 'uncommon' (*asādhāraṇa*)."
There is no inference [to establish this],
as it would be set aside by the contradiction of a universally accepted statement;
for instance, when one says "the hare-holder is not the moon" because it does not exist [as such], the intent of that statement is to reveal that it is not commonly known by the world at large.
There is no logical basis for establishing an inference that would cause those who lack faith to believe that the hare-marked [sign] is not the moon.
Therefore, this constitutes an error.
This treatise further states:
"It is just like the non-Buddhist Kāpālika."
This is called "Stringing Human Skulls into a Garland":
taking human skulls to fashion them into garlands for adornment.
When people mock this practice, [it is said:]...
He then establishes the formal argument (*pramāṇa*):
"Human skull-bone is pure;
because it is a part of a sentient being, this is the reason (*hetu*)."
Just as in the analogy of the conch shell,
although the probans and the example are without fault,
the thesis contradicts what is commonly regarded in the world as impure.
Therefore, this constitutes a fault.
Both of these are non-learner (aśaikṣa) and worldly (laukika);
they merely contradict what is common [to both].
Regarding the absence of self and other and so forth,
while the text speaks only of the whole,
logically there should also be cases where a portion is contradicted.
If one were to speak of them collectively, the hare-marked [moon] would not be the sun or the moon;
it would contradict common worldly consensus only with respect to the "one part" that is the moon,
whereas it does not contradict [the consensus regarding] the sun.
Question: Suppose, for instance,
that the Great Master traveled throughout the Western Regions and was about to return home, his studies complete.
At that time, King Śīlāditya,
who reigned over the five regions of India,
convened an eighteen-day *aviśeṣa-mahāpariṣad* (unrestricted great assembly).
He caused the Great Master’s established doctrine to spread throughout all of India;
he selected the worthy and virtuous to assemble at his location and dispatched the non-Buddhists and followers of the Hīnayāna.
They vied with one another to present their arguments and challenges.
When the Great Master established his formal syllogism (*pramāṇa*),
none among those present dared to respond or refute it.
The Great Master established the following inference for the Cognition-Only (Vijñaptimātra) doctrine:
"In ultimate reality, the color-form universally acknowledged [by both parties] is not separate from visual consciousness; this is the thesis (*pakṣa*).
The reason (*hetu*) is: because it is included within the first three [categories] as admitted by oneself, yet is not subsumed under the eye."
It is just like the analogy of visual consciousness.
Why does this not contradict worldly convention?
For it is commonly said in the world that form is distinct from consciousness.
Answer: Generally, in the methods of logic (*hetuvidyā*),
if there is a qualification within that which is to be established (*sādhyadharma*), [it must be explicitly stated].
Thus, there is no fault.
If one employs inference based on oneself (*svārthānumāna*),
the word "acknowledged" (*abhyupagata*) serves as a qualification.
This reveals that our own position is free from faults such as being "other" or "concomitant" and so forth;
whereas, in the case of an inference by another,
your own assertions would be excluded by the term "and so forth."
There is no fault such as contradicting one's own tenets and so forth.
If it concerns a common inference (*sādhāraṇa-anumāna*) and the like,
it is qualified by the term "from the perspective of ultimate reality" (*paramārthatas*).
There is no contradiction with worldly conventions, one's own teachings,
and so forth; for each case, there is a specific designation and distinction as appropriate.
In this inference,
because there is a specific qualification,
none of these faults apply.
There are teachings that claim [certain things] are real;
these clarify that they rely on the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya) and not on conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya).
Therefore, there is no contradiction with the non-learner worldly [convention].
Furthermore, this demonstrates that it is established based on the superior meaning of the Mahāyāna,
and not based on the Hīnayāna.
This does not contradict the teachings of the Āgamas and other scriptures that form exists apart from consciousness,
nor does it contradict the worldly consensus established by those who study the Hīnayāna.
It is a statement of universal acknowledgment.
Excluding the defiled forms of the last-birth bodhisattvas of the various Hīnayāna schools and all the contaminated forms of the bodies of all Buddhas,
if these were established as mere consciousness (vijñaptimātra).
Consequently, there would be the fallacy of partial non-establishment of one's own specific subject (*svadharmin-asiddha*),
as well as the fallacy of contradicting one's own tenet (*siddhānta-virodha*).
This is because the matter of the form (*rūpa*) of the Buddhas of the ten directions and the uncontaminated form (*anāsrava-rūpa*) of the Buddhas [would not be established].
He does not allow for its existence.
To establish it as being merely consciousness (*vijñaptimātra*) is unestablished because it lacks the aspect of being differentiated by another.
These two reasons—
In all such cases, there is a failure of the basis (*āśrayāsiddhi*) for at least one part [of the reason].
The term "universally acknowledged" (*prasiddha*) is employed to exclude these instances.
This is because the two [proponent and opponent] establish that all other forms (*rūpa*) commonly admitted by both are mere consciousness (*vijñaptimātra*).
Regarding the statement that they are "subsumed under the first three":
this indicates that among the eighteen elements (dhātus), which are divided into six groups of three, they are subsumed under the first three.
Otherwise, there would be an inconsistency.
This contradicts the fundamental tenet;
for it would mean that [the object] is not included within the first three [bases],
but is merely said to be "not included among the eyes."
There is then an inconclusive statement:
just as color, which is universally established, is not subsumed by the eye-consciousness,
it is nonetheless certainly not separate from the eye-consciousness.
Is it because, like [the other two], it is not subsumed by the five or three eyes?
Thus, matter that is universally established must necessarily be distinct from visual consciousness.
If you grant this, then because it is not subsumed by the five or three eyes...
Furthermore, it would contradict one's own tenet [to claim] that it is not separate from visual consciousness; therefore,
to avoid this fault, it is stated that they are "subsumed under the first three."
The phrase "not included among those perceived by the eye" also serves to exclude indeterminate cases and the contradiction of the specific characteristic of the phenomenon itself; that is to say,
were it not stated that they are "not included among those perceived by the eye," [the definition would fail to distinguish these].
However, because it is said to be subsumed under the first three [realms],
it is stated as an indeterminate term:
"matter that is universally established."
Is it like visual consciousness, which—
because it is subsumed within the first three [elements]— is necessarily not separate from visual consciousness?
Or is it like the visual faculty?
Because it is subsumed under the first three [stages], it is not necessarily dissociated from visual consciousness;
for the Mahāyāna masters state that those eye-faculties are not invariably and exclusively dissociated from visual consciousness.
Therefore, this is not determinate; it does not mean that [the object] is definitely not separated from visual consciousness.
One cannot say that it is definitely separated from visual consciousness.
This is a statement in which the method of operation contradicts its own characteristic.
Because it is real and universally established, visible form is not non-separate from visual consciousness;
because it is subsumed under the first three [bases],
just like the visual faculty.
Furthermore, there would be a definitive contradiction [with the definition].
To exclude these three faults, it is stated:
"because it is not included within the eye."
If that is so, why is it necessary to state one's own admission?
It is for the purpose of precluding the fallacy of contradicting the specific characteristics of the subject (dharmin).
Therefore, it is said that this is "admitted by oneself" (svasaṃmata),
not to indicate that it is "universally established" (prasiddha) as being subsumed within the first three [realms] of form.
It is not subsumed under the eye,
is not established by others,
and is accepted only by oneself.
That is to say, "color as it is truly and universally established" is a dharma with its own specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) that is not separate from visual consciousness.
This is the intrinsic characteristic of this dharma:
it is necessarily dissociated from eye-consciousness and visible forms, yet it is not necessarily dissociated from eye-consciousness and visible forms.
This is a distinction among existent phenomena (dharmas).
The proponent intends that form is not separate from visual consciousness;
the opponent then raises an objection based on a contradiction regarding this distinction.
Color that is conventionally established is not color that is inseparable from visual consciousness,
because it is subsumed under the first three [bases] while being non-subsumed by the eye,
just like visual consciousness itself.
To preclude this fault,
he says "admitted by oneself" (svābhyupagama),
thereby rendering that inference inconclusive (anaikāntika).
Is color, as it is commonly established,
like visual consciousness,
because it is included within the first three [aggregates] yet is not included by the eye?
It is not that visible forms are not separated from visual consciousness;
rather, it is because— just as you yourself admit regarding the visible forms of Buddhas in other realms—
they are subsumed under the first three elements (earth, water, and fire) and are not subsumed by the eye-faculty.
This is not separate from the visual consciousness and its objects.
If one does not claim it as a cause,
then it cannot be argued that the objects of the Buddhas in other directions constitute an inconclusive [reason].
Because these words would entail the fallacy of "one or the other" (anyatara-koṭi-pāta).
Since your proposed inference (anumāna) possesses this fallacy, it is invalid.
It is not the case that what is not real is indeterminate.
Generally, when one exposes the faults of another,
one must oneself be free from fault.
Since that which is established as real must necessarily lack any semblance [of contradiction],
it clarifies that there is no contradiction regarding the specific characteristics of the *dharmin* (the subject) in what was previously established; therefore,
it says "admitted by oneself" (*svayam-abhyupagata*).
However, there was the Dharma Master Shunjing of Silla,
whose reputation resounded throughout the Tang and Tubo regions, whose learning encompassed both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna,
and whose practice was devoted to the teachings of Kāśyapa.
In every practice, he adhered to the dhūtas;
his mind was intent on minimizing attachments,
and he constantly exhorted himself toward few desires.
Thereafter, his cultivated arts spread through the Western Xia,
and his teachings illuminated the Eastern Barbarians;
his reputation and Way flourished daily.
Both monastics and laypeople held him in deep reverence;
though there were many eminent masters like dragons and elephants,
he was frequently praised abroad as being peerless in his time.
Regarding this inference, it establishes a definitive contradiction.
In the year of Qiandeng,
he sent a request for the Master’s explanation, saying:
Because it is truly established, color must be distinct from visual consciousness;
for you yourself admit that it is included within the first three [bases] but not included within visual consciousness,
just like the eye faculty.
At that time, he spoke for the sake of clarification.
Generally, regarding the methods of *hetuvidyā* (logic), if it is one's own inference (*svārthānumāna*), [one should state: "It is so."
In the case of the thesis, reason, and example, one must rely on what is accepted by oneself;
the same applies to what is accepted by others or by both.
One establishes [these] based on what is accepted by oneself, others, or both.
The same must also apply to the case of opposition;
thus, it is called the "Excellence of Reasoning" (Hetuvidyā) because it is free from error.
As previously stated, this refers to "consciousness-only" (vijñaptimātra).
While this was based on common inference (*sādhāraṇa-anumāna*),
it now relies on autonomous [inference] (*svatantra*).
Thus, all forms of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) are subject to this contradiction.
For example, a disciple of the Buddha, in opposition to the proponents of the theory that sound is produced (*śabdotpattivādin*),
establishes that sound is impermanent because it is a product (*kṛtakatvāt*).
For example, like a jar or other such objects.
Proponents of the theory that sound is produced argue that sound is eternal because it possesses the nature of being audible.
Just as the nature of sound is admitted by oneself,
it would necessarily contradict the aforementioned proof;
since that [proof] is not established, [the argument fails].
Therefore, based on one's own [inference],
it is not possible to formulate an inference in opposition to what is common [to both parties].
Furthermore, once the thesis (*pakṣa*) is established as being based on what is common, it is said to be "universally acknowledged" (*prasiddha*).
Because the reason is stated as something admitted by oneself,
it does not conform [to the opponent's position].
Furthermore, the reason would suffer from the fallacy of being unestablished for at least one party (*anyatarāsiddha*).
The Mahāyāna does not accept this,
because they themselves admit that it is not subsumed under visual consciousness,
as its cause operates upon common form (*sādhāraṇa-rūpa*).
Furthermore, the common example also suffers from the fallacy of the unestablished probandum (*sādhyāprasiddhi*):
the visual faculty (*cakṣur-indriya*) of the Mahāyāna is not necessarily dissociated from visual consciousness (*cakṣurvijñāna*).
The faculties are the cause and consciousness is the fruit;
since they are neither identical nor separate,
how much more so is this the case for the wisdom that accomplishes activities?
It universally conditions the eye-faculty as its remote object-condition (ālambana-pratyaya) for the eye-consciousness that takes it as its cognitive object.
There is the sense of being definitively separated;
furthermore, this statement is established by one's own admission based on common inference (*sādharmya-anumāna*).
This refutes the opponent's claim that there is a contradiction regarding the distinction between other dharmas.
The opponent states, "It is admitted by oneself," which reveals that,
according to one's own inference, it is not subsumed within visual consciousness (*cakṣurvijñāna*).
How could these possibly be consistent?
Furthermore, both the thesis (*pakṣa*) and the example (*dṛṣṭānta*) of that inference rely on common [experience],
whereas only the logical reason (*hetu*) relies on the specific [subject].
Since they all contradict one another,
although subtle words have been raised by all,
they cannot yet serve as a guiding manual.
It is fortunate that you have been able to carefully examine the preceding text;
this should indeed suffice as the ultimate logical conclusion.
Above, we have extensively discussed the tenets of our own school as a digression.
Since the treatise itself specifies that these are "true," there is no fault of contradicting worldly convention;
as stated above, they are termed "non-learnerly worldly."
The two types of learners are worldly,
for they are commonly known by the multitude of practitioners;
if one were to deviate from these two meanings, both profound and superficial, [the teaching would be lost].
Both are termed "contradictory to one's own teaching.
If it contradicts only the superficial meaning,
it may also be termed "contradictory to the world."
The profound meaning is subtle and suspended;
because it is not something commonly known in the world,
there are also fourfold alternatives (catuṣkoṭi) regarding its being complete or partial.

Whether these are faults or not is explained in the section on "Contradiction with One's Own Teachings," for that which contradicts the world of practitioners necessarily contradicts one's own teachings.
In this treatise, there are only instances that contradict [the principle] of being "not learned" and "entirely worldly";
other cases are to be determined accordingly.
Generally, if a thesis is proposed as being ultimate (paramārtha), [it must be examined].
As stated in the *Tattvasiddhi*:
"In ultimate reality, conditioned phenomena are empty,
because they arise dependently like illusions."
The unconditioned has no reality;
its non-arising is like a flower in the sky.
Furthermore, there are no faults such as contradicting one's own teachings or common worldly consensus.
Treatise:
Regarding contradiction with one's own words, it is as when one says, "My mother is a barren woman.
Commentary:
The basis of the thesis consists of the property (dharma) and the locus of the property (dharmin).
The locus of the property is the substantial entity (svabhāva).
"Dharma" is its meaning;
the meaning relies upon that essence and does not conflict with it.
They may be established in mutual conformity.
Now, by saying "my mother," it is clearly known that there is a son.
Furthermore, the mention of a "barren woman" clarifies that she definitively has no child; thus,
the nature of my mother is identical in meaning to that of a barren woman.
There are phenomena and their attributes that do not rely upon or accord with one another;
since your own words are already contradictory,
what can you possibly establish when facing an opponent?
Therefore, it is an error.
"Stone woman" (*śilāputraka*) should properly be translated as "barren woman" (*kūṭastha*);
however, following ancient translations, the term "stone woman" has been retained.
The *Nyāyamukha-śāstra* states:
"For example, it is like establishing that all speech is false.
This refers to a non-Buddhist (tīrthika) who establishes that all speech is entirely illusory and false."
Dignāga raises an objection:
"If, as you say, all statements are false,
then your own statement that accords with reality must also be false."
Since it is not false,
as one part is real,
this would contradict the statement that all phenomena (dharmas) are such.
If what you say is itself false,
then other words are not false;
thus, what you now say is a falsehood.
It is not that you falsely claim what is false;
rather, your own words are false,
while the words of others are not false.
This would thus contradict the fundamental tenets and all such statements would be false;
therefore, it is called "contradiction with one's own words.
If there is reliance upon the teachings, this is termed "one's own words."
Within this, there are also two types of fourfold propositions (catuṣkoṭi): those consisting of the whole and those consisting of a part.
Regarding the fourfold proposition of the whole:
there is that which contradicts one's own words but not those of others.
For example, as the Lokāyatikas say in their discourse on emptiness:
"The four great elements are without reality.
They assert that the four great elements must not be without reality.
That which is said to be without reality must certainly not be the four great elements,
because it contradicts one's own teaching and one's own words, rather than those of another.
There are cases where one contradicts the words of another but not one's own;
for example, when a follower of the Buddha’s Dharma speaks to a Sāṃkhya, saying:
"That self of yours is not an experiencer."
That which he describes as the self must certainly not be non-experiencer;
if it were a non-experiencer,
it would certainly not be that self.
Therefore, there are statements that contradict the teachings of others but not one's own;
there are also statements that contradict both one's own and others' teachings,
such as the claim that "all speech is false."
These various propositions exist only in dependence upon contradicting the teachings;
therefore, this particular proposition is likewise identical to the aforementioned contradiction with one's own teaching.
The meaning should be understood accordingly.
Within the two sets of four propositions,
there are those that contradict both the particular and the universal.
All these are subsumed under these faults.
Among those that contradict what is common,
contradicting others is not a fault.
To contradict one's own [position] constitutes a fault;
therefore, this is designated solely as "contradiction by one's own words.
Even if both [positions] are not contradicted, they are not subsumed under this fault.
Since two identical [positions] must necessarily coincide and be established as such,
it is also subsumed under the fault [of contradiction];
it merely contradicts the other [party].
This is not subsumed under the category of "general fallacy," because it fundamentally involves harming others;
this statement is definitively self-contradictory.
There are also cases where both [reasons] or either one in its entirety are subject to doubt, as well as contradictions with one's own words;
fearing prolixity, I shall cease here,
but these will be fully demonstrated in the section on "Unestablished" (*asiddha*).
Treatise:

Regarding the case where the predicate (*viśeṣya*) is not established for both parties, it is as when a follower of the Buddha establishes to a Sāṃkhya teacher that sound is subject to destruction. Commentary: *The term "not established" refers to the following: when one party asserts a thesis regarding a subject that is accepted by both, yet the predicate is not accepted by the opponent, this is called "the predicate being unestablished. For example, when a Buddhist disciple asserts to a Sāṃkhya teacher that "sound is subject to destruction," the predicate "subject to destruction" is not established for the Sāṃkhya.*
If divided into two sections:
the first clarifies the semblance of antiquity,
and the second clarifies the semblance of the present.
Now it appears there are two [positions].
The first three lack a basis;
the last one accords with the meaning.
If categorized into three sections,
the first five reveal the departure from the Dharma,
clarifying the meaning of contradiction.
The next three [verses] reveal that [the self] does not exist,
clarifying the non-existence of its basis at the beginning of the kalpa of formation.
A non-Buddhist teacher emerged,
named Kapila, which in this language means "the Yellow-Red-Colored Rishi."
Because his beard, hair, and facial complexion were all yellowish-red, he was called the Rishi Kapila; this is a corruption of the ancient name.
His disciples thereafter...
Among the eighteen schools,
the foremost is named Vārṣagaṇya;
this means "Rain."
Because they arise during the rainy season,
their followers are called the Rain-Hosts (Vārṣagaṇya).
In Sanskrit, they are called Sāṃkhyasattva-tantra.
This is called Sāṃkhya.
It means that one repeatedly evaluates all phenomena through wisdom;
the discourse (sūtra) arises from this enumeration (saṃkhyā).
This treatise can generate the *sāṃkhya*;
it is therefore also called *Sāṃkhya*. Those who study this treatise are known as the Sāṃkhyas.
Furthermore, those who propound that [system] are called the Sāṃkhyas;
they teach twenty-five principles (tattva).
Briefly, there are three;
in the middle, four;
and extensively, twenty-five principles (tattvas).
Briefly, there are three types:
namely, intrinsic nature,
transformation, and [the third].
That which I know is the self-nature;
the ancients called it the "dark nature" (mingxing).
That which has not yet attained greatness and so forth is called *svabhāva* (intrinsic nature);
that which is about to attain greatness and so forth is also called *pradhāna* (the primal source),
because it is preeminent and ancient.
"Transformation" refers to the twenty-three principles (tattvas) in the intermediate stage;
it does not mean that their substance is newly produced.
"Because it is transformed by the fundamental self-nature;
'I, the knower' refers to the *puruṣa* (the spiritual self)."
Because that which is able to experience objects possesses wondrous function;
as for the middle [category], it is fourfold:
first, it is fundamental and not subject to transformation.
This refers to intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
It is called "fundamental" (*mūla*) because it can bring others into existence;
since it is not brought into existence by another, it is not subject to transformation. That which is subject to transformation is not fundamental.
This has two meanings.
One interpretation holds that there are sixteen truths,
namely the eleven faculties and the five great elements.
The second [classification] consists of eleven types.
Excluding the five great elements (*mahābhūta*),
these possess both an original nature and undergo transformation.
There are also two meanings.
One says there are seven truths, namely:
the great self-grasping (*mahātmagrāha*) and the five subtle elements (*tanmātra*).
The second [classification] consists of twelve kinds;
that is, the previous seven plus the five great elements.
They are called "fundamental" because they are able to bring others into existence.
It is called "transformation" (pariṇāma) because it arises for the sake of others.
The fourth is neither original nor transformation;
this refers to the *puruṣa* (the self).
Because it cannot be produced by another, nor is it produced by itself,
[the cause] is extensively categorized as the twenty-five principles (*tattva*).
The first is primordial nature (*prakṛti*).
Two great elements;
three types of self-grasping;
four kinds of *vāyu*; five *dhātu*s.
5. The five great elements;
6. the five faculties of cognition;
7. the five faculties of action.
The eighth is the faculty of equanimity of mind;
the ninth is the one who knows "I am.
Regarding these nine dharmas:
It is expanded into twenty-five principles (*tattva*).
That is to say, the first is primordial nature (*prakṛti*),
which is collectively termed "primordial nature."
It is also called the "Three Qualities" (triguṇa), because each of sattva,
rajas, and tamas possesses three kinds of qualities.
The initial term is *sattva*,
which here means "sentient being" (*sattva*) as well as "valiant" (*vīra*).
In this context, the sense of "valiant" is adopted.
*Raśa-yun-mi* (剌闍云微) is also called *ch'en-p'en* (塵坌); here,
we take the meaning of "dust."
The answer is: *mā* means darkness.
It is the darkness of dullness.
Its primary etymological definition is the darkness of the dust of passion (*rajas*).
Regarding the three qualities (*guṇas*):
according to ancient terminology, they are called passion (*rajas*), coarseness (*tamas*), and darkness (*kṛṣṇa*);
in the present terminology, they are called yellow, red, and black.
The former were named joy, sorrow, and equanimity;
the present are named greed, hatred, and delusion.
The former were named pleasure, pain, and delusion.
Now, these are named pleasure, pain, and indifference;
because these three qualities are the causes of saṃsāra,
the nature of the Puruṣa is liberation.
I contemplate the supreme object;
through the transformation of the three qualities (guṇas), I experience it.
Bound by the objects of perception,
one cannot attain nirvana;
later, one comes to feel weary of them and cultivates the path.
Since the self is not conceptualized and its intrinsic nature is unchanging,
the self is free from the bondage of objects.
One then attains liberation.
The twenty-three truths in between,
although impermanent, are subject to transformation.
There is no arising or ceasing;
the self-nature of the divine self (puruṣa) may exist or not exist according to its function.
Its essence is eternally abiding; yet,
among all worldly phenomena, there is no dharma that undergoes destruction or decay,
as explained at length in the *Saptati-śāstra* (Seventy Verses on Gold) and the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-ṭīkā*.
Now, the Buddha’s disciples, in opposition to the Sāṃkhya teachers,
establish that sound is subject to destruction;
it is a sound that possesses the nature of a dharma.
Although both parties may concede this,
it destroys the principles of one's own school and is not established for the other party.
Since the world does not exist,
there would be no basis for either the general or the particular;
therefore, one must further establish [a foundation].
Because it is not the True Teaching (Shinjō),
it constitutes an error.
Such meanings as these have all been explained above.
Regarding this, there are four permutations concerning the whole and the part.
As for the four permutations of the whole:
there is that which is unestablished in its own differentiator but not in another’s.
For example, as the Sāṃkhya teachers said to the disciples of the Buddha:
"The five objects, such as form and sound, manifest through the transformation of consciousness;
although these phenomena such as form are commonly established by both [parties]."
The manifestation of the ālayavijñāna is not something that exists within its own system;
since it possesses the capacity to distinguish others, it cannot be established as non-self,
as stated in the treatise.
If one posits that sound perishes as soon as it arises,
there is no proof for either [the existence of sound or its distinction from other things],
just as when a Sāṃkhya teacher argues against a Buddhist disciple.
The five [aggregates] beginning with form are said to be subsumed under the category of qualities (*guṇa*),
because in this world and the next, they are not subsumed under the category of non-qualities (*aguṇa*).
Regarding the "one part of four propositions":

Question: Among these nine fallacies, are there any that contradict direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), and are there also any that contradict inference (*anumāna*)?
Answer: There are indeed those that contradict direct perception.
Is this also consistent with what is universally established?
Thus, there are eight sets of four propositions regarding a single instance of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).
Likewise, there are seven [sets of four propositions] regarding a single instance of inference (*anumāna*).
Up to the point where neither is fully established— there being one [case] for each—
this totals thirty-six sets of four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*).
In answering these nine fallacies, there are the categories of self, other, both together, neither together nor separately, and the whole versus the part.
From this, there are four permutations for each pair of opposites.
There is that which contradicts perception but is not [contradicted by] inference,
such as the claim that sound is not audible.
There are [inferences] that contradict inference but not perception,
such as saying "a jar is permanent.
There are also [inferences] that contradict both perception and inference.
For example, when a Hīnayāna master posits against a Mahāyāna proponent that the various forms of the sense-bases of tangibility (*spraṣṭavyāyatana*) are not necessarily apprehended by the mind,
this contradicts direct perception but does not contradict his own scripture;
just as contradicting another’s direct perception does not constitute a contradiction of one’s own scripture.
There are cases that contradict one's own teaching but do not contradict direct perception,
such as when the Vaiśeṣika masters establish that sound is eternal.
There are also cases that contradict both direct perception and one's own teaching.
All that contradicts one’s own direct perception necessarily contradicts one’s own scripture; thus,
there may be things that contradict direct perception yet are not worldly,
just as there are things that contradict one’s own direct perception yet are not non-learnerly (aśaikṣa) worldly phenomena.
There are cases that contradict worldly convention but do not contradict direct perception,
such as saying "the hare-bearer is not the moon.
There are also cases that contradict both direct perception and worldly convention.
As it is said, "sound is not audible," this contradicts direct perception and is a self-contradiction,
just like contradicting the direct perception of another.
There is contradiction with one's own words that is not contradicted by direct perception,
such as saying, "All speech is false.
There is also contradiction with direct perception as well as with one's own words.
Just as contradicting what is manifest necessarily involves contradicting one’s own scripture and one’s own words,
there are cases of contradicting what is manifest that do not constitute a "non-establishment of the differentiator" (*asiddha-viśeṣaṇa*),

There are cases where a reason is unestablished (asiddha) but does not contradict perception (pratyakṣa),
such as when one establishes the perishability of sound against a Sāṃkhya opponent.
There are also cases where a reason both contradicts perception and is unestablished.
For example, while contradicting only one's own perception or another's may result in the non-establishment of the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*),
if it contradicts what is commonly perceived, the qualifier must necessarily be established. Thus,
there are cases where something contradicts perception yet the qualified object (*viśeṣya*) is not unestablished.
Just as sound is not something that is heard,
[if one were to say] "there is a distinction," it would not be established, yet it would not contradict direct perception.
It is like saying to a disciple of the Buddha, "I am volition."
There is also the fallacy of the unestablished nature of the object of negation (*viśeṣya-asiddha*) regarding contradiction with one's own perception;
just as there is the fallacy of the unestablished nature of the object of negation regarding contradiction with one's own perception,
if there were contradiction with a common perception, the object of negation would necessarily be established.
There are cases where [a reason] contradicts direct perception but is not unestablished in both [the proponent’s and opponent’s systems],
such as "sound is not audible.
There are also cases where [a reason] is unestablished in both systems but does not contradict direct perception.
Just as when one speaks of a "self" in relation to the Buddha-dharma as being the cause of a composite,
it contradicts direct perception and is unestablished for both [parties];
just as it contradicts one's own direct perception and is unestablished for both oneself and others.
If one contradicts what is commonly perceived by both parties, it necessarily becomes established as such;
thus, there are contradictions with what is perceived that do not accord with consensus,
such as [the claim] that sound is not audible.
There are cases where [a cognition] accords with what is manifest but does not contradict it,
such as the sound that is heard.
There are also cases where it contradicts what is manifest while still accords with it.
Just as contradicting one's own existence implies the meaning of conforming to another,
so too the Vaiśeṣika school posits that qualities such as cognition and pleasure are not within the domain of the self.
If one contradicts what is commonly manifest, it necessarily does not accord with the facts.
Thus, even down to cases where both [proponent and opponent] fail to establish [the reason], there is no accord with the facts;
for example, when one says in response to the Buddha’s Dharma: "I take the self to be the causal condition for the synthesis [of the aggregates]."
There are cases where the [reason] is consistent with the thesis but not jointly unestablished,
such as "sound is audible.
There are also cases where it is both jointly unestablished and consistent with the thesis.
This means that [the reason] is unestablished for both parties and is also contradictory to the opponent's own position.
Thus, there are thirty-six fourfold permutations (*catuṣkoṭi*) in total.
Is it possible for there to be a contradiction with direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), as well as contradictions with inference (*anumāna*) and one's own scriptures (*āgama*)?
When combined with direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), there are twenty-eight sets of four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*);

Treatise: That which occurs in one part of the similar class (*sapakṣa*) but occurs throughout the dissimilar class (*vipakṣa*) is, for example, as when it is said: "Sound is not non-produced by volitional effort, because it possesses the nature of impermanence. Commentary: * **Similar Class (*Sapakṣa*):** This refers to the locus where the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*) is known to exist with certainty. For instance, in the case of the inference "Sound is impermanent," the similar class consists of things such as pots, where both the reason (*hetu*)—being produced by volitional effort—and the property to be proven—impermanence—are known to exist. * **Dissimilar Class (*Vipakṣa*):** This refers to the locus where the property to be proven is known to be absent with certainty. In the same example, the dissimilar class consists of things such as space (*ākāśa*), where both the reason and the property to be proven are known to be absent. * **Occurring in One Part of the Similar Class:** This means that within the similar class, the reason is present in some instances but absent in others. For example, among the similar class (impermanent things), sound is produced by volitional effort, whereas lightning is not. Thus, the reason "being produced by volitional effort" applies to only a portion of the similar class. * **Occurring Throughout the Dissimilar Class:** This means that the reason is entirely absent from the dissimilar class. In the example, since all permanent things (the dissimilar class) are necessarily not produced by volitional effort, the reason is "pervasive" across the entire dissimilar class. Because this reason is thus distributed, it is called a "contradictory reason" (*viruddha-hetu*). Specifically, it contradicts the thesis by proving the opposite of what was intended; in this case, it proves that sound *is* produced by volitional effort. Therefore, it is a fallacy. The phrase "because it possesses the nature of impermanence" is cited here to illustrate how the reason is distributed across the two classes. The commentary explains that while the reason is partially present in the similar class, it is universally present in the dissimilar class, thereby rendering the argument invalid.

Question: Are these various "indefinites" (*anaikāntika*) partial or complete?
Answer: There is no logical principle that exhausts [the matter], and therefore [they are both].
Among the fifty-four types of inconclusive reasons previously mentioned,

there are various types of "self-inconclusive" (*svasādhāraṇa-anaikāntika*) and "common inconclusive" (*sādhāraṇa-anaikāntika*) reasons within both the self-inference (*svārthānumāna*) and the common inference (*parārthānumāna*).
This is an inconclusive fallacy (*anaikāntika-doṣa*). It is a common error;
it is not a genuine proof (*sādhana*).
What is meant by "refuting another"?
It refers to cases within another's inference where there is an inconclusive reason (*anaikāntika*) that is either "unrestricted" (*asādhāraṇa*) or "common" (*sādhāraṇa*).

This is also the fallacy of inconclusiveness (*anaikāntika*). Since it establishes contradictions for the opponent and commits the fallacies of being contradictory to oneself (*svaviruddha*) and common to both (*sādhāraṇa*),
it cannot function as a valid refutation.
How can these constitute a valid proof?
Within one's own inference,
all such [reasons] adduced by others are inconclusive.
In his system of inference,
all cases of "uncertainty regarding the self" (svāsiddha) are not included among the fallacies.
The purpose of establishing a thesis is fundamentally to contradict and harm another; thus,
while all that one establishes for oneself is not [necessarily] accepted by others, what others establish is not necessarily non-existent [for oneself].
Establishing the other as non-self,
while self is indeterminate and not [self];
in accordance with what is appropriate, all is to be understood according to reason.
This treatise, for the time being, explains this based on the fallacy of the "uncertainty common to both" (ubhayāsiddha).
This is because it treats as a fallacy a reason that both the proponent and the opponent agree upon regarding two examples— whether they be common or uncommon.
Although the two examples are shared,
if the reason follows only one of them,
then due to doubt regarding the reason, the concordant example lacks its essential nature.
Accordingly, this is subsumed under the fallacy of the "inconclusive" (*anaikāntika*), which arises from the failure to establish the basis for any one of the alternatives;
it comprises fifty-four types of inconclusive fallacies.
Since there are four types for each,
they constitute two hundred and sixteen kinds of fallacies of non-determination (*aniyata-doṣa*).
If the four [reasons] are not established, there are twenty-seven cases— comprising the whole or a part of the existence or non-existence of the entity— as admitted by both oneself and others.
All are to be understood according to the preceding explanation.

Regarding these twenty-seven fallacies and fifty-four various types of inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) fallacies, each one possesses a total of one thousand four hundred and fifty-eight kinds of inconclusive fallacies; as the *Nyāyamukha* states:
The four types of non-establishment [of the reason] should also be stated accordingly, depending on whether [the reason] exists, does not exist, or both, within the similar instances (sapakṣa).
Therefore, it is known.
The principle is certainly thus.
However, the *Nyāyamukha* summarizes this verse as follows:
"If a dharma is unique..."
It contradicts common consensus;
as it applies to all phenomena,
it is entirely of the nature of a cause for doubt.
The four types of uncertain causes (*anaikāntika-hetu*) are subsumed within the similar and dissimilar instances (*sapakṣa* and *vipakṣa*),
as appropriate to each case.
Because they are shared either in their entirety or in part,
they do not contradict one another as being "unshared" (exclusive); rather, each includes only one [of the two].
These six types of inconclusive reasons apply universally to all propositions;
they are causes for doubt regarding all such phenomena, not merely within the propositions mentioned above. They are termed "inconclusive" (anaikāntika) in this general sense.

The portion of this volume of the *Nyāyapraveśa-śāstra* was completed on the third day of the ninth month in the second year of the Kenmu era. Due to the imperial prayers for the state, I was summoned to the Jōkōdō at the Daijō-in to recite the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra*; because the task was assigned to six persons, the progress of the transcription was delayed and the work was only finished upon its conclusion.

Relying on the merit of crushing heterodoxy, the myriad nations have returned to the correct principle; through the divine assistance of the *Hetuvidyā*, the One Man governs with virtuous administration.

Having finished reading it once, having finished reading it once, I, the provisional *Vinaya* Master, read this during the leisure following my medicinal bath on the twenty-third day of the same month. Completed:
the *Commentary on the Nyāyapraveśa-śāstra*, Volume Lower.
This treatise was composed by the Śramaṇa Ji of the Great Ci’en Monastery.

There are four types of contradiction: namely, the contradictory reason regarding the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of the property (*dharma*), the contradictory reason regarding the specific characteristic of the mode of the property (*dharmaviśeṣa*), the contradictory reason regarding the specific characteristic of the locus (*dharmin*), and the contradictory reason regarding the specific characteristic of the mode of the locus (*dharmiviśeṣa*), and so forth.
The commentary states:
Third, the explanation of contradictions has three parts;
first is the heading.
Next comes the enumeration;
later comes the explanation.
These are the first two.
Regarding the meaning of "contradictory reasons":
this refers to two theses being mutually opposed;
these constitute the four fallacies.
Without altering the original reason,
it causes the established thesis to become contradictory,
because it serves as a reason that is contrary to the [intended] property.
This is called the "contradiction of names.
It is a contradiction of names because the cause receives the name of its effect;
it is not a contradiction of the thesis that constitutes a "contradiction."
Therefore, the absence of a thesis also contradicts the reason;
this constitutes a refutation by means of an example.
As stated in the *Nyāyamukha*:
If a factor can establish a thesis that is contradictory [to what was intended],
it is the fallacy of contradiction;
this is termed a "pseudo-reason" (*hetvābhāsa*).
Just as with non-contradictory [reasons],
the same applies to contradictory ones;
for there is no certainty regarding the property to be proven (sādhyadharma), as it does not exist.
Because of that statement, the reason (hetu) remains fixed as before,
while the example (dṛṣṭānta) may be modified accordingly;
thus, the four fallacies mentioned below [apply].
The first instance modifies the analogy;
the latter three remain as before.
Question: There is a reason for returning to the original thesis.
It does not accord with the meaning of the reason;
the reason is contradictory,
and the thesis is also contrary to the reason.
This does not accord with the fundamental tenets;
it should be called a "contradiction.
Answer: Because the reason establishes a thesis that causes the thesis to contradict itself.
Because the reason contradicts its own name,
it does not establish the thesis;
rather, it causes the reason to be reversed.

These are not called "contradictions. Furthermore, that which is termed a contradiction regarding the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of a phenomenon (*dharma*) is based on the reason (*hetu*),
whereas that which is termed a contradiction with inference (*anumāna*) is based on the thesis (*pakṣa*).
Because they are categorized separately,
contradictions are divided into four types;
while the contradiction of the thesis (*pakṣa*) is explained collectively.
It is only the inference based on names that contradicts [the thesis].
Since the thesis is judged by the reason,
one knows that there is also a distinction regarding the property (dharma).

There is the contradiction of the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of the subject (*dharmin*), and there is the contradiction with inference (*anumāna*) regarding the specific property (*viśeṣa*) of the subject.
If this were not so, why would one speak only of the contradiction with inference regarding the intrinsic nature of the subject?
Are the *viruddhāvyabhicārin* (the contradictory-undetermined) and the *viruddha-hetu* (the contradictory reason) each of four types?
In this school, the teaching of dharmas is briefly of two kinds:
first, intrinsic nature (svabhāva);
second, differentiation (viśeṣa).
This has three layers.
The first is the distinction between the restricted and the universal, as expressed in the *Abhidharmasamuccaya* and other treatises.
That which is established as intrinsic nature refers to the intrinsic nature of the self and the intrinsic nature of phenomena.
Because that which is established [as either] existent or non-existent possesses a distinct nature in each case.
As for the distinctions,
they refer to the distinction of self and the distinction of phenomena.
Whether it be all-pervasive or not all-pervasive,
whether permanent or impermanent.
Whether with form or without form—
such are the immeasurable distinctions,
according to what is appropriate for each case.
Space and so forth are omnipresent;
form and so forth are not omnipresent.
Because the former is restricted while the latter is pervasive, there is a distinction between the two.
Second is the sequence of priority and posteriority.
Within a composite aggregate,
that which is presented first is termed its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
What is called "subsequent exposition" is termed "differentiation," because that which is presented later serves to distinguish what preceded it.
The *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra* states:
Their treatise on logic (*hetuvidyā*) differs from this regarding specifically characterized (*svalakṣaṇa*) and generally characterized (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*) phenomena;
they assert that all dharmas are each distinct and localized within their own intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
That which is called the "specific characteristic" (svalakṣaṇa) is that which penetrates through others like a thread threading through flowers;
this is called the "common characteristic" (sāmānyalakṣaṇa).
Therefore, based on this,
the restricted essence of sound and so forth is termed "intrinsic nature" (svabhāva),
while impermanence, which pervades others, is termed "differentiation" (viśeṣa).
The designation is not fixed.
If one establishes that all five aggregates are without self,
then the five aggregates are termed "self-characteristics."
The distinction between "I" and "non-I" is termed differentiation.
If one says "I am volition," then volition is the differentiation.
I am the self-nature;
therefore, it is not fixed.
When examined through reasoning, this is so.
Although this is indeed the same as the preceding [section],
the teaching differs slightly and the meaning is also distinct.
It is divided into two sections.
Third is the "Statement of Consent," which sets forth what is expressed within the statement itself.
The preceding category and the subsequent pervasive category are both termed "intrinsic nature" (svabhāva). Therefore,
both phenomena (dharma) and the possessors of phenomena (dharmī) possess intrinsic nature.
That which is established as a distinct meaning intended by one's own mind is called a "differentiation" (viśeṣa). Therefore,
both the property (dharma) and the locus of the property (dharmin) possess differentiation.
It is not that all [theses] are accepted;
the meaning is as previously explained.
Now, it will be shown that there is a reason which causes these four types of established theses to result in the opposite of what was intended.
Therefore, they are called "reasons contradictory to the specific characteristic of the dharma" (*dharmasvalakṣaṇaviruddhahetu*) and so forth.
When the treatise uses the word "etc.
(*ādi*), it is intended to indicate other distinct types of reasons.
The types of opposition to the thesis do not exceed these four;
therefore, the treatise speaks only of four kinds of contradiction.
The reasons capable of opposing [the thesis] consist of fifteen categories.
There are four [cases] for contradicting one;
that is, each contradicts individually.
There are six [cases] for contradicting two.
That is to say: contradicting the first two;
contradicting the first three;
contradicting the first four.
Contradicting two and three;
contradicting two and four;
contradicting three and four.
Contradiction with three [of the four] exists in four cases;
that is, by mutually excluding one.
Contradiction with four [of the four] exists in one case.
Thus, fifteen [points] are established.
In the treatise, only the first two are shown to individually contradict one cause,
while the latter two are shown to collectively contradict two causes.
By citing these three types, the others—namely the twelve—are included;
therefore, the word "etc. (ādi) is used.
[End of] Treatise.

Among these, an "antithesis to the specific characteristic of the property" (*dharmasvalakṣaṇaviruddhahetu*) is, for example, as when one says: "Sound is eternal, because it is produced," or "because it is produced immediately following volitional effort.
The commentary states:
The following provides a detailed explanation of the four [categories].
The initial section consists of three parts.
First, the titles are listed.
Next, the reason for the thesis is revealed;
subsequently, it would result in a contradiction with the meaning.
These are the first two [points].
Question: There are four types of contradiction.
Why, then, is the intrinsic characteristic of the dharma stated first?
Answer: Because it is the primary point of contention.
Contradiction with superior inference (*āgamaviruddha*) and contradictory certainty (*viruddhāvyabhicārin*) both exclusively state the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of that dharma.
Regarding that initial statement,
there are two masters here,
as in the theory of the production of sound (*śabdotpatti-vāda*).
The proponent of the thesis that sound is eternal establishes "the property of being produced" as the reason.
The proponent of the theory that sound is manifested establishes "the property of being produced immediately following volitional effort" as the reason.
Commentary:
This reason is contradictory because it exists only within the dissimilar class (*vipakṣa*).
Explanation: [As follows].
This results in a contradiction with the intended meaning,
because the initial thesis of permanence takes space and so forth as its similar instances (*sapakṣa*).
Vases and the like serve as the dissimilar instances (*vipakṣa*).
The reason (*hetu*) of "being produced" (*kṛtakatva*) is entirely absent from these similar instances (*sapakṣa*).
It is present throughout the dissimilar instances (*vipakṣa*);
this is the fourth of the nine types of reasons (*navavidhahetu*).
One should formulate a counter-inference (*pratikūla-pramāṇa*) as follows:
Sound is impermanent,
because it is produced.
For example, like a jar and so forth;
according to the second thesis,
space serves as the similar instance (sapakṣa).
Taking batteries and the like as the heterogeneous instances (*vipakṣa*),
the reason— being produced by volitional effort—
is entirely absent from those similar instances (*sapakṣa*).
It exists in the dissimilar class (vipakṣa), such as lightning, and in things like non-pots;
this is the sixth of the nine types of reasons (navavidhahetu).
These two reasons, conversely,
establish impermanence,
because they contradict the specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) of the properties as stated in your own thesis.
This is called the reason of contradictory names (*nāma-viruddha-hetu*). Therefore, the *Nyāyamukha* states:
"With respect to that which exists in both [the similar and dissimilar instances]..."
Non-existence in another [instance] is the non-reason (*anaikāntika*).
The opposite of this is called the contradictory (*viruddha*).
All others are the indeterminate (*anaikāntika*).
This reason of "being produced" (kṛtakatva) is the reverse of the second correct reason among the nine positions;
it exists in the similar class (sapakṣa) and does not exist in the dissimilar class (vipakṣa).
Since this [reason] is absent in the similar class (sapakṣa) but present in the dissimilar class (vipakṣa),
this "cause of effort" (prayatnaja-hetu) is the reverse of the eighth valid reason among the nine types of reasons.
It exists in the similar class (sapakṣa) and does not exist in the dissimilar class (vipakṣa);
it neither exists nor does not exist in this [subject] which is both the similar and the dissimilar class.
This has already been discussed repeatedly above.
I shall not elaborate further here.
This "semblance-reason" (hetvābhāsa) continues to employ the traditional [categories].
The analogy was revised and established first;
the latter three reasons, however,
have both their reasons and analogies as original.
Due to these four reasons,
the cause must remain as it was;
the analogy remains the same even if the particulars are altered.
If it were not so, there would necessarily be no case where a phenomenon's own-characteristic could coincide with either of the other two [characteristics],
such that it could constitute a contradiction between the two causes.
It is granted that the first [example] is modified as a metaphor,
but the latter three are not modified.
Furthermore, among the nine types of reasons, the fourth and the sixth are termed "contradictory reasons" (*viruddha-hetu*).
It must be either identical and non-existent,
or different and existent, or both;
whichever [position] one establishes.

Regarding the latter three [types of contradictory reasons], since they are established based on direct observation and the reason exists in the similar class (*sapakṣa*), how can it be further objected that they fail to establish contradiction?
The *Nyāyamukha* merely states: "If a property can establish what is contradictory to the probandum..."
This is the fallacy of contradiction (*viruddha*),
which is termed a "pseudo-reason" (*hetvābhāsa*).
It is not stated that the similar example (*sapakṣa*) should likewise still employ the old [subject].
This treatise demonstrates the Dharma:
the first [section] employs a modified analogy,
while the latter three rely upon the original.
This is intended to lead students to understand that the reason is determinate,
so as not to commit the aforementioned fallacy regarding the example;
this applies to the three reasons mentioned below.
Although the establishment [of the position] may appear to be achieved through observation,
it actually results in contradiction; thus,
one must investigate each point thoroughly.
All of these are likewise only identical and not different,
for to do otherwise would result in contradiction;
this shall be understood in detail below.
Question: According to the proponents of phonetics (śabdavādin), your statement that "sound is impermanent" should not itself be sound;
for it possesses the property of being produced (*kṛtakatva*).
Like a jar, a basin, and so forth.
Is this second correct reason not a contradiction of the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of the subject (*dharmin*)?
Answer: That is not an over-inclusive fault.
For example, when one establishes that sound is impermanent, "impermanence" is the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of the property (*dharma*).
If the reason established were to conversely prove that sound is permanent,
then this would indeed constitute such a fallacy.
Now, since both the property-possessor (*dharmin*) and the property (*dharma*) are cited together as the "property-possessor of the property," this fault does not apply;
rather, this is merely a fallacy of similarity through conceptual differentiation (*vikalpa*).
Because of this transgression, both [the reason and the thesis] are unestablished.
This is because the reason of "being produced" (kṛtakatva) is not accepted by either the proponent or the opponent as being based on impermanence.
Because arising and ceasing are distinct,
even if they were to grant that there is a basis,
one would still incur a fault in at least one of the two cases.
Furthermore, since impermanence does not exist,
the "produced nature" which depends upon it would also commit the fallacy of the unestablished locus (*āśrayāsiddha*).
Should there be an objection stating:
"If your sound is impermanent, it should not be the case that 'sound is impermanent,' because you yourself admit that it is impermanent."
As in the case of "a jar is impermanent," this too is not a fault,
because there is no such characteristic of a fault in these cases that resemble a formal proof (*sādhana*).
The claim that sound is impermanent is the fundamental point of contention.
"Sound" is the subject (dharmin);
it is not the property (dharma) intended by the proponent.
It cannot be said that this is a fault of differentiating dharmas,
nor is it subsumed under "contradictory indeterminacy" (*viruddhāvyabhicārin*),
because it is not a fundamental dispute (*mūlavivāda*).
If one were to concede that all the aforementioned [objections] constitute fallacies,
then it would follow that there are no valid reasons for any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
Consequently, one would fail to perceive any fault in what appears to be a formal proof (*sādhanābhāsa*).
All of these are fallacious refutations;
this shall be understood below. [End of] Treatise.

Regarding the "reason that contradicts the specific property of the subject" (*dharmaviśeṣaviruddhahetu*): for example, it is said that "the eyes and so forth must exist for the sake of another because they are composite in nature, like bedding.
The commentary states:
according to the preceding [analysis], there are also three [types].
These are the first two.
Generally, when two distinctions are termed "contradictory," it does not mean that the expression stated is excluded from the locus of the property (dharmin).
All other meanings are merely distinctions (*viśeṣa*).
Only when two opposing positions each establish their respective claims through appropriate reasons,
such that there is a distinct meaning intended by the mind and subject to dispute, can it be called a distinction.
Because it causes contradiction,
it is called a contradictory reason (*viruddha-hetu*).
If it were not so, [it would not be a contradictory reason].
For example, when one establishes the thesis that sound is impermanent,
there are properties such as being audible or inaudible pertaining to sound,
and regarding impermanence itself, there are properties such as being its causal condition or not being its causal condition.
All such cases are termed "contradictory.
Because the reason brings about contradiction, it is called that [contradictory] reason. If this is so, then:
Thus, there is no contradiction with the meaning of the "contradictory reason" (*viruddha-hetu*).
All cases such as "contradiction by inference" (*anumāna-viruddha*) should be explained according to this principle.
The meaning here is as follows:
if the Sāṃkhya non-Buddhists, in opposition to the disciples of the Buddha,
intend to establish that the self (ātman) is the experiencer.
One employs the eyes and so forth.
If the self were an existent entity that employs the eyes and so forth,
there would be a failure to establish the specific property (*viśeṣa-asiddha*) within the thesis (*pakṣa*).
The cause consisting of accumulated nature is unestablished for both parties,
just like the analogy of bedding.
The thesis is unestablished.
If one says that the eyes and so forth must exist for the sake of the self,
the qualification is unestablished.
The lack of a similar instance (sapakṣa) [renders] the reason of "being an aggregate" contradictory to the specific characteristic (svalakṣaṇa) of the subject (dharmin).
The analogy of bedding-furniture fails to establish the point to be proven.
If it were established that the eyes and so forth exist for the sake of another as mere designations,
this would be a case of proving what is already universally accepted.
By means of this expedient, he falsely establishes a thesis, saying:
"The eyes and so forth must exist for the sake of another.
Herein, the eyes and so forth are the subject (*dharmin*).
Pointing directly to things to manifest and explain them;
employing dharmas for the sake of others;
and skillfully revealing them through expedient means.
The mind is established as necessarily being a distinction of phenomena;
it does not accumulate other things,
but is the real self that experiences.
If it is explicitly stated that "it is not accumulated for the use of another," the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) is unestablished,
and the thesis (*sādhya*) is likewise unestablished.
Furthermore, there is an absence of a similar instance (sapakṣa),
and the reason (hetu) contradicts its own specific characteristic (sva-lakṣaṇa);
therefore, it must be established through skillful means.
The cause of accumulation:
because many atoms accumulate to form the eye and so forth,
as in the analogy of bedding.
Since those things such as beds and seats are composite in nature and are both admitted by [the opponent and ourselves] to be for the enjoyment of others,
they may serve as a valid corroborative example (*dṛṣṭānta*).
The method of using examples through causes should not be differentiated;
therefore, they are established collectively.
Treatise.

Just as this reason can establish that the eyes and so forth must necessarily exist for the sake of another, it likewise establishes the contradictory specific characteristic of the thesis to be proven: that they exist for the sake of an aggregate.
The commentary states:
There are two ways in which this constitutes a contradiction of meaning;
first, the presentation of the specific causes for the phenomena being contradicted.
This is the first [section] explaining the reasons for what follows.
The initial text consists of two parts.
This reason is like that which can establish that the eyes and so forth must necessarily exist for the sake of another.
This restates the preceding reason, which is capable of establishing the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*).
"In this way, it is also able... and so forth.
Furthermore, it is revealed that this reason can also serve as a contradictory cause for the specific distinctions of those phenomena.
According to the Sāṃkhya teacher,
the five phenomena such as the eye [and the other sense organs]—
These are the five faculties of cognition;
bedding and seats are phenomena composed of the five subtle elements (*tanmātra*).
They do not accumulate [the view] of another,
namely that there is a real self (ātman) whose essence is eternal and primordially existent.
That which is accumulated by others is the conventionally designated self established in dependence upon the eye and so forth;
it is impermanent and subject to transformation.
However, the sense organs such as the eye do not possess the excellence of a real self that is accumulated from others;
rather, they directly experience these five subtle elements (tanmātra).
It is based upon the eye and other organs that a conventional self is established.
Therefore, since my faculties such as the eyes are inferior for the purpose of accumulation,
those requisites such as bedding must necessarily be contemplated and utilized by the conscious self (ātman).
Therefore, they are established in sequence beginning with the "great" [elements] and so forth.
If one considers the self as real, its function is superior;
if one considers the self as provisional, its function is inferior.
Nevertheless, one employs the provisional self to settle into what is required before accepting a seat;
thus, regarding bedding and requisites,
the use of the provisional self is superior to that of others.
In truth, my own capacity is inferior; now,
Dignāga employs that very same reason.
It contradicts the distinctions of superiority and inferiority among established phenomena;
it is neither the intrinsic characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of phenomena nor any of the various distinctions pertaining to phenomena.
In all cases, this constitutes a contradiction.
Therefore, the treatise merely states that it contradicts the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*).
First, it restates the preceding reason (*hetu*), which is capable of establishing the specific characteristic of the property to be proven, as follows:
The previously mentioned reason of being an aggregate (saṃcita) can establish that the subjects (dharmin) such as the eye, as posited by the Sāṃkhya school,
must necessarily have their own-characteristic (svalakṣaṇa) as something used for the sake of another.
This refers precisely to that reason (*hetu*).
In this manner, it is also capable of establishing the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of the property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*) to be proven.
It intends to refute the meaning of the contradictory distinction [of the opponent], namely, that [the collection] has a different purpose from its constituent parts.
The thesis exists for the sake of another;
this is the specific characteristic (svalakṣaṇa) of that dharma,
which is what is intended by the proponent regarding this specific characteristic.
Accumulating for the sake of others and not accumulating for the sake of others:
these are the distinctions among dharmas.
The cause for that accumulation remains unchanged even now;
it is precisely by means of that [cause] that the distinction of the intended dharma is established as being for the sake of another's accumulation.
Because bedding and such things possess the nature of being accumulations, they are designated as "self" by way of convention,
since the usage of the term is predominant for that which is an accumulation.
Since the eyes and so forth are likewise of an aggregative nature, they should—
like bedding— be considered as "aggregates" in the sense of being conventional designations for a superior functional utility (*adhiṣṭhāna-viniyoga*).
If one does not raise this objection regarding such a superior functional utility, [the argument fails].
In this regard, one's own thesis would entail the fallacy of "proving what is already established" (*siddhasādhana*),
because the opponent also admits that the eyes and so forth are aggregates functioning for the sake of another.
One may merely raise the objection that [the thesis] is superior in its function as a designation for another.

One must not raise the objection that "the reality of my [position] is inferior," for this would contradict one's own tenets and because there is no similar instance (*sapakṣa*) within a common inference (*sādhāraṇa-anumāna*).
If all forms of inference based on others (*parārthānumāna*) were not excluded,
then the various masters of the Western Regions who are unskilled would simply state the fault of "contradiction with a specific characteristic" (*viśeṣaviruddha*).
The eyes and so forth would then have to serve as an aggregate for the use of another;
the reason and the example are the same as before.
The Sāṃkhya objects, saying:
Your thesis is consistent with [the opponent's] position.
Who has ever said that the eye and so forth do not function as an accumulation?
Furthermore, it is explained in the Western Regions (India) as follows:

Although I, Jun-kō, have entered the chamber of my late teacher and received his final instructions, my realization remains distant from the gateway of correct principle; thus, I am unfit to transmit the lamp of the Dharma. Furthermore, whenever I peruse the three volumes of the Great Commentary (*Mahāṭīkā*), I lose track of the beginning and end of the text, and when I occasionally consult the various masters of the two dynasties, I am bewildered by the depth and shallowness of their interpretations. Nevertheless, relying upon the grace of His Highness the Lord [Chōja], who entrusted me with the elucidation of the clear exegesis, I have respectfully followed the teachings of my late teacher.
